headline: Race Point slack tide, a bent rod, and a 38-pound bass that wouldn't quit
subhead: While the water south of the Cape pushes bass into deep, nocturnal patterns, the Bay stays cool enough to keep the bite honest in daylight — and this week proved it again.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, dead slack at Race Point, and I had a guy from Worcester in the stern who'd never felt a striper pull like that before. We'd drifted the rip three times with nothing but a couple of short bluefish to show for it, and I was about to pull the mackerel and try Peaked Hill Bars instead. Then the current started to build again off the last of the ebb, that first hint of push you feel in your palms before you see it in the water, and his rod loaded up like someone hung a truck tire on it. Thirty-eight pounds, fat as a football, came up out of that green water with a mackerel still hanging out the corner of her jaw. That's the rip doing what it's supposed to do — you just have to be patient enough to let the tide tell you when.

That's been the story of the Bay all week. While the fish south of us — down through the Sound, off Jersey, along most of the coast — have gone deep and noctural on account of that low-to-mid-70s surface water, we're not dealing with that problem up here. The Bay holds its temperature better than open coastline, and that's kept our bass willing to feed in daylight on the rips instead of sulking until dark. I've been telling guys at the co-op the same thing for two weeks now — the water stays cooler north of the Cape, and it shows. We flagged this pattern last week, said conditions would stay steady through stable water, and that's exactly what played out. No surprises, just consistent work if you put the time in.

Race Point remains the money spot on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the new flood — that window where the rip stands up and the mackerel schools get pushed and squeezed against the structure. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, 20-pound fluoro leader, just enough weight to keep bottom contact without killing the natural swim — that's been the ticket for the better fish, 28 to 40 pounds. If you can't get mackerel, bunker chunks fished on the bottom in 40 to 60 feet will still draw strikes, just don't expect the same class of fish.

Peaked Hill Bars has been more of a bluefish show this week, and a good one — three- to six-pound choppers thick on the surface during the last hour of daylight, chewing through peanut bunker pushed up against the bar. Poppers and Deadly Dicks worked fast across the top get hit hard. There's bass mixed in underneath that blitz too, but you have to slow down and get a bucktail or a swimming plug down through the chaos to connect with them — the blues will eat first if you let them.

Billingsgate has quieted some for the cod compared to earlier in the summer, but it hasn't shut off. I marked scattered fish on the deeper edges, 65 to 80 feet, drifting clam baits and diamond jigs tipped with squid strips on the last of the incoming tide when the current slows enough to hold bottom without a pound of lead. Nothing to write home about — a few fish in the 8 to 12 pound range for guys who put in a full tide's worth of drifting — but it's honest work if cod is what you're after and you're not expecting a pile.

Fluke have been the most dependable thing going off Sandy Neck and down toward Barnstable Harbor, holding on the sandy flats in 15 to 25 feet where the tide runs clean over clam and mussel bottom. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the outgoing, have been putting keepers in the box mixed with plenty of shorts — steady rather than spectacular, which is about right for early August. If you want a numbers day with a shot at a few dinner fish, that's where I'd send you.

The moon's building toward new phase over the next several days, and that means stronger tides pushing through both rips by the weekend. If that current comes in clean and doesn't get blown out by any weather moving through, I'd expect Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars to fish better than they have all week — bigger pushes of water usually mean bigger pushes of bait, and bigger bait means bigger bass showing up to eat it. That's the pattern I've watched play out for thirty years on this water, and I don't see a reason it breaks now. Worth planning a morning around the building flood at Race Point if the wind cooperates. I'll have mackerel rigs ready either way.
